focus.claude: LATENT KNOWLEDGE THAT IS LOST ("knows but does not say"). Generations 10-11 showed visible reasoning habits are symptoms; look instead for cases where the network internally prefers the RIGHT option and a specific later component overrides it. Concretely: on MIXED and WRONG traces, take forced-answer probes ('So the answer is (') at several points of the thinking and read them through the layers (logit lens on the residual stream at L12-L23 projected onto the option letters, or per-layer direct attribution). Look for a systematic pattern: gold ranked higher at an intermediate layer than at the output, and one or a few late components (an MLP neuron group, a head, a direction) that push it down, e.g. by favouring the option already named most often, the familiar-sounding one, or the model's pre-thinking prior. If such an override exists and is content-independent, weaken it and show on HELD-OUT prefixes (not used to fit) that P(gold) rises before spending generate passes. If no override exists (gold is never preferred internally on wrong traces), say so clearly: that is an important negative result.
focus.ed_f: OPEN CHOICE. You are a new editor this generation (no earlier reports of your own). Read the history in this file first: four mechanism-targeted edits in generations 10-11 were real but did not move accuracy, and the noise floor is about +/-4 points. Pick the target you judge most likely to raise P(gold) on held-out probes, and justify the choice in notes.md before spending passes. Candidates the other editors suggested but did not test: (a) replace a hedging or exam-gaming paragraph with a neutral content paragraph in fixed traces and see if P(gold) moves (cause vs symptom); (b) act at the SOURCE of the generic 'first item of a list' feature (the residual direction written at list items) rather than in one head; (c) a gate on uncertainty that steers toward re-deriving content ('Let us recall the definition...') rather than suppressing words; (d) anything else the evidence points to, e.g. option-content comparison errors on two-finalist questions, or the 21 never-right questions if some of them are reasoning slips rather than missing knowledge. Apply the gate rule: show P(gold) rises on held-out prefixes before you generate.
